1:1.t: Ramathaim-zophim is Ramah (1:19). "Ephraimite": the KJV's "Ephrathite", here meaning a man of Ephraim. "Hill country of Ephraim": the KJV's "mount Ephraim".

1:5.t: "A double portion": the KJV's "a worthy portion". The Hebrew is unclear; it may mean a portion fit for an honored person.

1:6.t: "Her rival": the KJV's "her adversary", meaning the other wife, Peninnah.

1:9.t: "Temple": the KJV's word for the house of the LORD at Shiloh, here still a tent shrine with buildings around it.

1:16.t: "Worthless woman": the KJV's "a daughter of Belial" (see Original language).

"Worthless" (Hebrew beliyaal, the KJV's "Belial"): the word probably means "without worth" or "good for nothing". The KJV treats it as a name, "sons of Belial", and later Jewish writers and Paul (2 Corinthians 6:15) did use Belial as a name for Satan. In Samuel it describes scoundrels and troublemakers, so we translate it rather than leave it as a name.

1:20.t: Samuel sounds like the Hebrew for "heard by God" and "asked of God".

1:24.t: KJV: "one ephah of flour". "Skin of wine": the KJV's "bottle". "Three bulls": the KJV's "three bullocks"; the Greek Old Testament reads "a three-year-old bull", which fits the single bull of verse 25.

1:28.t: "Giving him to the LORD": the KJV's "lent him to the LORD". The Hebrew verb is the same as "asked" in verse 27, a play on words: the child she asked for she now gives back for life.

2:1.t: "Strength": the KJV's "horn", a picture of strength and honor taken from a strong animal's horns.
"My mouth mocks my enemies": the KJV's "my mouth is enlarged over mine enemies", meaning opened wide in triumph.

2:10.t: "Strength": the KJV's "horn", a picture of strength and honor taken from a strong animal's horns.

"Anointed" (Hebrew mashiach): one marked out with oil for an office, here the king. Messiah comes from this word, and Christ from its Greek translation, Christos. Hannah speaks of a king before Israel has one; Christians have also heard in her words a promise of the Messiah. We keep "anointed" so the reader can see the link without the text deciding it.

2:8.t: "Ash heap": the KJV's "dunghill", the town refuse pile where beggars sat.

"Anointed" (Hebrew mashach, the verb behind mashiach; see 2:10): pouring oil on Saul's head marked him out as chosen by God. From this point the king is "the LORD's anointed", a title that makes his person sacred (24:6).

9:24.t: "Thigh": the KJV's "shoulder"; the Hebrew means the upper leg, a choice portion.

9:26.t: "On the roof": the flat roof of the house, where guests often slept.

10:5.t: "Harp, tambourine, flute and lyre": the KJV's "psaltery, and a tabret, and a pipe, and a harp".

10:12.t: "Who is their father?": prophets were often called sons of a leading prophet, their "father"; the question may mean that a prophet's gift does not depend on who his father is.

10:20.t: "Chosen by lot": the KJV's "taken". The choice was made by casting lots before the LORD.

10:25.t: "The rights and duties of the kingship": the KJV's "the manner of the kingdom".

10:27.t: After this verse one ancient Hebrew scroll from Qumran adds a paragraph about Nahash's cruelty to the tribes east of the Jordan. The KJV does not include it, and neither does this translation.

11:11.t: "Before dawn": the KJV's "in the morning watch", the last watch of the night, from about two to six in the morning.

12:3.t: "To make me look the other way": the KJV's "to blind mine eyes therewith".

13:1.t: "Saul reigned one year, and when he had reigned two years": as in the KJV. The Hebrew reads literally "Saul was a year old when he began to reign, and he reigned two years over Israel"; the numbers seem to have dropped out of the text, and modern Bibles fill them in different ways.

13:4.t: "Hateful": the KJV's "had in abomination", literally "became a stench".

13:5.t: "30,000 chariots": as in the Hebrew and the KJV. Some Greek manuscripts read 3,000.

13:12.t: "Asked for the LORD's favor": the KJV's "made supplication unto the LORD", literally "softened the face of the LORD".

13:20.t: "Plow blades": the KJV's "coulters". 13:21 "They had only a file": as in the KJV. The Hebrew word (pim) puzzled the KJV translators; inscribed weights found since show it was a weight of silver, about two-thirds of a shekel, so many modern Bibles read that the Philistines charged a pim for sharpening.

14:29.t: "His eyes brightened": the KJV's "his eyes were enlightened", meaning he was refreshed.

15:2.t: "I will punish": the KJV's "I remember", meaning God now acts on what He remembers.

15:3.t: "Devote to destruction", "destroy completely": the KJV's "utterly destroy" (see Original language).

"Devote to destruction" (Hebrew herem, the KJV's "utterly destroy"): herem means to set something apart wholly for God by giving it up to destruction, so that no one may take it for personal use. The same idea lies behind Jericho (Joshua 6:17-19) and Achan's sin (Joshua 7). Saul's fault in this chapter is that he and the people kept part of what was devoted. We use "devote to destruction" where the sense of something given over to God matters, and "destroy completely" elsewhere.

15:8.t: "Devote to destruction", "destroy completely": the KJV's "utterly destroy" (see Original language).

15:18.t: "Devote to destruction", "destroy completely": the KJV's "utterly destroy" (see Original language).

15:20.t: "Devote to destruction", "destroy completely": the KJV's "utterly destroy" (see Original language).

15:9.t: "Fattened calves": the KJV's "fatlings". "Worthless and weak": the KJV's "vile and refuse".

15:11.t: "Was angry": the KJV's "it grieved Samuel"; the Hebrew means he was hot with anger or deeply upset.

"I regret", "change His mind", "regretted" (Hebrew nacham; see Genesis 6:6): the same verb is used three times in this chapter. God "regrets" making Saul king (15:11, 35), yet Samuel says God does not "change His mind" like a man (15:29). The verses do not contradict each other: God truly grieves over human choices, but He does not go back on His word or decide on a whim as people do.

15:12.t: "Monument": the KJV's "a place"; the Hebrew word means a hand, here a marker or memorial. Carmel here is a town in Judah, not Mount Carmel.

15:23.t: "Divination": the KJV's "witchcraft", seeking hidden knowledge by forbidden means. "Idolatry": the Hebrew is teraphim, household idols (see Genesis 31:19).

15:29.t: "The Glory of Israel": the KJV's "the Strength of Israel", a title of God; the Hebrew means lasting glory or endurance.

25:13.t: "Strap on his sword": the KJV's "gird ye on".

25:17.t: "Worthless man": the KJV's "son of Belial" and "man of Belial" (see 1:16).

25:25.t: "Worthless man": the KJV's "son of Belial" and "man of Belial" (see 1:16).
Nabal means "fool", in the sense of one who is morally senseless.

25:18.t: KJV: "five measures of parched corn" (five seahs). "Skins of wine": the KJV's "bottles".

25:22.t: "One male": the KJV's "any that pisseth against the wall", a coarse old expression for a male.

25:34.t: "One male": the KJV's "any that pisseth against the wall", a coarse old expression for a male.

25:29.t: "Bundle of the living": the KJV's "bundle of life", a picture of a treasure kept safe in a pouch. "The pocket of a sling": the KJV's "the middle of a sling".

25:31.t: "Burden on his conscience": the KJV's "offence of heart".

25:35.t: "Granted your request": the KJV's "accepted thy person", literally "lifted up your face".

25:44.t: Palti: the KJV spells it Phalti. He is called Paltiel at 2 Samuel 3:15.

26:5.t: "Inside the camp": the KJV's "in the trench", the ring of wagons around the camp (see 17:20).

26:7.t: "Inside the camp": the KJV's "in the trench", the ring of wagons around the camp (see 17:20).
"Near his head": the KJV's "at his bolster". "Jug": the KJV's "cruse".

26:11.t: "Near his head": the KJV's "at his bolster". "Jug": the KJV's "cruse".

26:16.t: "Near his head": the KJV's "at his bolster". "Jug": the KJV's "cruse".

26:15.t: "Are you not a man?": the KJV's "Art not thou a valiant man?"

26:19.t: "May He accept an offering": the KJV's "let him accept an offering", that is, let me make peace with God by sacrifice. "Go, serve other gods": to be driven out of the LORD's land was, in effect, to be cut off from His worship.

27:3.t: "Of Jezreel", "of Carmel": the KJV's "the Jezreelitess", "the Carmelitess". "Nabal's widow": the KJV's "Nabal's wife".

27:8.t: Girzites: the KJV's "Gezrites"; the Hebrew text has both readings.

27:10.t: "The Negev": the KJV's "the south", the dry southern region of Judah. "Where did you raid": the KJV's "Whither have ye made a road", where "road" is an old word for a raid.

28:2.t: "My bodyguard": the KJV's "keeper of mine head".

28:3.t: "Mediums" and "spiritists": the KJV's "those that had familiar spirits" and "wizards", people who claimed to consult the dead. The law forbade them (Leviticus 19:31, Deuteronomy 18:10-11).

28:7.t: "Mediums" and "spiritists": the KJV's "those that had familiar spirits" and "wizards", people who claimed to consult the dead. The law forbade them (Leviticus 19:31, Deuteronomy 18:10-11).

28:6.t: "Urim" (Hebrew urim, with thummim): objects kept in the high priest's breastpiece (Exodus 28:30) and used to ask God for a yes-or-no answer. The words may mean "lights" and "perfections". How they worked is not known. That God answered Saul neither by dreams, Urim nor prophets means every lawful way of hearing from Him was closed.

28:13.t: "Divine beings": the KJV's "gods"; the Hebrew elohim here means a being from the spirit world (see Genesis 1:1).

28:14.t: "Robe": the KJV's "mantle", the same kind of robe Samuel wore at 15:27.

28:19.t: "With me": that is, among the dead.

29:3.t: "Deserted to me": the KJV's "fell unto me".

29:6.t: "March out and in with me": the KJV's "thy going out and thy coming in", meaning taking part in the campaign.

30:14.t: Cherethites: a people living near the Philistines, perhaps from Crete. Their men later served in David's guard (2 Samuel 8:18).

30:6.t: "Found strength in the LORD": the KJV's "encouraged himself in the LORD".

30:9.t: "Ravine": the KJV's "brook", a stream bed that is dry most of the year.

30:21.t: "Ravine": the KJV's "brook", a stream bed that is dry most of the year.

30:22.t: "Wicked and worthless men": the KJV's "wicked men and men of Belial" (see 1:16).

30:27.t: "Ramoth of the Negev": the KJV's "south Ramoth".

30:29.t: Racal: the KJV spells it Rachal. The Greek reads Carmel.

30:30.t: Bor-ashan: the KJV spells it Chor-ashan.

30:31.t: "Roamed": the KJV's "were wont to haunt", that is, used to go.

31:9.t: "Temples of their idols": the KJV's "the house of their idols".

31:10.t: "The temple of the Ashtoreths": the KJV's "the house of Ashtaroth" (see 7:3). Beth-shan is also spelled Beth-shean.

31:13.t: "Under a tree": as in the KJV. The Hebrew names it a tamarisk.

1:3.t: "The LORD of hosts" (Hebrew YHWH Tsebaoth, Sabaoth): this title first appears here. Tsebaoth means armies, and the "hosts" are the armies of Israel (17:45), the stars, and the angels of heaven. The title presents the LORD as commander of every power in heaven and on earth. We keep the KJV's "LORD of hosts" because "hosts" covers all three better than "armies".

1:15.t: "Soul" (Hebrew nephesh; see Genesis 2:7): Hannah pours out her whole self before God.

2:35.t: "Anointed" (Hebrew mashiach): one marked out with oil for an office, here the king. Messiah comes from this word, and Christ from its Greek translation, Christos. Hannah speaks of a king before Israel has one; Christians have also heard in her words a promise of the Messiah. We keep "anointed" so the reader can see the link without the text deciding it.

2:18.t: "Ephod" (Hebrew ephod): a priestly garment, probably a kind of apron or vest. The high priest's ephod held the breastpiece with the Urim and Thummim (Exodus 28), and in Samuel "the ephod" is often the means of asking God for guidance (23:9, 30:7). The plain linen ephod worn by Samuel and by the priests of Nob (22:18) was simpler. Elsewhere an ephod could be a cult object (Judges 8:27). We keep the Hebrew word.

2:21.t: "Came to Hannah's aid" (Hebrew paqad, the KJV's "visited"): when God "visits" in the Old Testament, He comes to act, either to help or to punish. Here it means He gave Hannah what she longed for (compare Genesis 50:24).

8:7.t: "They have rejected Me from being King over them": Israel already had a king, the LORD Himself (Judges 8:23). The request for a human king "like all the nations" is treated as turning away from Him, though God then grants it and works through it.

9:9.t: "Seer" (Hebrew roeh, "one who sees") and "prophet" (Hebrew navi, probably "one who is called" or "one who speaks for another"): the verse explains an old word to later readers. Both describe a person through whom God makes His will known.

10:6.t: "The Spirit of the LORD will come upon you with power" (Hebrew ruach, "spirit"; the verb tsalach, "rush, come mightily"): ruach is explained at Genesis 1:2. The verb pictures a sudden, overwhelming coming, the same word used of Samson (Judges 14:6). In Samuel the Spirit comes on a person to equip him for a task, and can also depart (16:14). The KJV's "came upon" is kept, with "with power" added to carry the force of the verb.

10:10.t: "The Spirit of the LORD will come upon you with power" (Hebrew ruach, "spirit"; the verb tsalach, "rush, come mightily"): ruach is explained at Genesis 1:2. The verb pictures a sudden, overwhelming coming, the same word used of Samson (Judges 14:6). In Samuel the Spirit comes on a person to equip him for a task, and can also depart (16:14). The KJV's "came upon" is kept, with "with power" added to carry the force of the verb.

11:6.t: "The Spirit of the LORD will come upon you with power" (Hebrew ruach, "spirit"; the verb tsalach, "rush, come mightily"): ruach is explained at Genesis 1:2. The verb pictures a sudden, overwhelming coming, the same word used of Samson (Judges 14:6). In Samuel the Spirit comes on a person to equip him for a task, and can also depart (16:14). The KJV's "came upon" is kept, with "with power" added to carry the force of the verb.

15:35.t: "I regret", "change His mind", "regretted" (Hebrew nacham; see Genesis 6:6): the same verb is used three times in this chapter. God "regrets" making Saul king (15:11, 35), yet Samuel says God does not "change His mind" like a man (15:29). The verses do not contradict each other: God truly grieves over human choices, but He does not go back on His word or decide on a whim as people do.

15:22.t: "To obey" (Hebrew shema, "hear, listen"): the same word means to hear and to obey. "To listen is better than the fat of rams" makes the point that hearing God's voice and acting on it is the true worship that sacrifice is meant to express.

16:7.t: "Heart" (Hebrew lev): in Hebrew the heart is the center of thought, will and character, not mainly the feelings. When God looks on the heart, He sees the whole inner person.

16:13.t: "The Spirit of the LORD came upon David with power ... the Spirit of the LORD departed from Saul" (Hebrew ruach; see 10:6): the two verses are deliberately set side by side. The Spirit that had equipped Saul for kingship now rests on David, and Saul is left troubled.

18:1.t: "Jonathan loved him as his own soul" (Hebrew ahav, "love"; see Genesis 22:2; nephesh, "soul"; see Genesis 2:7): "as his own soul" means as himself, echoing "love your neighbor as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18). In this period ahav was also used of loyalty between a king and his followers or between covenant partners, so "love" here includes devoted allegiance. Jonathan's love is sealed with a covenant (18:3, 20:16) and with gifts of his robe and weapons, the signs of his own claim as Saul's heir. We keep the KJV's plain "loved".

18:3.t: "Jonathan loved him as his own soul" (Hebrew ahav, "love"; see Genesis 22:2; nephesh, "soul"; see Genesis 2:7): "as his own soul" means as himself, echoing "love your neighbor as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18). In this period ahav was also used of loyalty between a king and his followers or between covenant partners, so "love" here includes devoted allegiance. Jonathan's love is sealed with a covenant (18:3, 20:16) and with gifts of his robe and weapons, the signs of his own claim as Saul's heir. We keep the KJV's plain "loved".
"Covenant" (Hebrew berit): a binding agreement sworn before God, with promises on both sides. David calls it "a covenant of the LORD" (20:8) because the LORD is its witness and guarantor.

20:17.t: "Jonathan loved him as his own soul" (Hebrew ahav, "love"; see Genesis 22:2; nephesh, "soul"; see Genesis 2:7): "as his own soul" means as himself, echoing "love your neighbor as yourself" (Leviticus 19:18). In this period ahav was also used of loyalty between a king and his followers or between covenant partners, so "love" here includes devoted allegiance. Jonathan's love is sealed with a covenant (18:3, 20:16) and with gifts of his robe and weapons, the signs of his own claim as Saul's heir. We keep the KJV's plain "loved".

20:8.t: "Covenant" (Hebrew berit): a binding agreement sworn before God, with promises on both sides. David calls it "a covenant of the LORD" (20:8) because the LORD is its witness and guarantor.

"Kindness", "steadfast love" (Hebrew hesed; see Genesis 24:27): loyal covenant love. Between David and Jonathan it is "kindness" (20:8, 20:15), but "the steadfast love of the LORD" (20:14) is God's own faithful love, which Jonathan asks David to copy toward him and his house forever, so it takes the rendering used for God's hesed. David keeps this promise to Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9:1, 9:7).

20:14.t: "Kindness", "steadfast love" (Hebrew hesed; see Genesis 24:27): loyal covenant love. Between David and Jonathan it is "kindness" (20:8, 20:15), but "the steadfast love of the LORD" (20:14) is God's own faithful love, which Jonathan asks David to copy toward him and his house forever, so it takes the rendering used for God's hesed. David keeps this promise to Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9:1, 9:7).

24:6.t: "The LORD's anointed" (Hebrew meshiach YHWH; see 2:10 and 10:1): for David the anointing makes Saul untouchable, even though God has rejected him and he is trying to kill David. To strike the anointed king would be to strike at the One who anointed him. David repeats this at 26:9-11 and acts on it at 2 Samuel 1:14-16.

24:10.t: "The LORD's anointed" (Hebrew meshiach YHWH; see 2:10 and 10:1): for David the anointing makes Saul untouchable, even though God has rejected him and he is trying to kill David. To strike the anointed king would be to strike at the One who anointed him. David repeats this at 26:9-11 and acts on it at 2 Samuel 1:14-16.

28:12.t: Samuel at Endor: the text says plainly that the woman saw Samuel and that Samuel spoke. Interpreters differ: many hold that God allowed Samuel himself to appear, which explains the woman's terror; others think it was a deceiving spirit in his likeness. The passage is not an approval of consulting the dead, which the law forbids and which is listed among Saul's sins in 1 Chronicles 10:13.
